_comment: DEV/TEST FIXTURE ONLY, never bundled. The compiled mission exactly as the bridge serves it from GET /api/missions/trajectory, generated with `go run ./cmd/eniac-bridge mission compile --config ../../deploy/config/config.dev.yaml ../../missions/trajectory.yaml` (from src/bridge). tests/web/contract.test.ts checks it against missions/trajectory.yaml.
title: Trajectory
summary: Fire a cannon shell, one dot at a time.

text.headline: Tell ENIAC the card was read
text.body: ENIAC takes in numbers from punched cards. When the reader finishes, it sends a signal. Tap the reader OUT jack on the Initiating Unit. Then tap program trunk 1-2.
text.more: Cards were how numbers got into ENIAC. A card had 80 columns. The card in this mission holds seven numbers of up to 10 digits.
text.done: Now the reader can tell the machine it is done.

hints.wrongFrom: That jack belongs to another job. We want the reader, OUT.

text.headline: Punch the hop number
text.body: Each card will say which hop it is: 1, 2, 3 and so on. The printer has a switch for each part of the card. Tap the glowing switch 6 and choose P, for punch.
text.more: The punch worked in 16 groups of 5 columns. A switch for each group chose what got punched. On our card, you will see the hop number, how far along the shell is, and how high.
text.done: Now each card will carry its hop number.

hints.wrongSwitch: That switch is for another part of the card. Try the glowing one.
hints.wrongValue: Blank leaves the number off. Choose P.

text.headline: Wire up the card punch
text.body: On each hop, ENIAC punches a card. The signal to punch rides on program trunk 2-5. Tap trunk 2-5. Then tap the Pi jack on the Initiating Unit, the punch input.
text.more: When a card is punched, the Initiating Unit sends a done signal, and ENIAC carries on. The punch took a little over half a second per card.
text.done: Now each hop will punch a card.

hints.wrongTo: That jack starts something else. We want the punch, IN: Pi.

text.headline: Is the shell still flying?
text.body: After each hop, ENIAC checks the shell's height. If the shell is still in the air, Accumulator 19 sends a signal. Tap its 5-out jack. Then tap program trunk 1-4.
text.more: Accumulator 20 holds the shell's height. The program checks its sign. While the height is above zero, the signal says keep going. When it drops below zero, the shell has landed.

byTarget.a19.6o: That jack is for the other answer, landing. We want 5, out.

text.headline: Start the next hop
text.body: The 'keep going' signal must start another hop. The Master Programmer, ENIAC's conductor, runs the hops. Tap program trunk 1-4. Then tap the H jack on the Master Programmer.
text.more: The Master Programmer had ten steppers, each counting stages and handing off to the next, a bit like a music box with pins. This one is the stepper for the hop loop.
text.done: Hop after hop, ENIAC will fly the shell. Your cables made the loop!

hints.wrongTo: That jack is for a different stepper. Look for H.

briefing.headline: The path of a shell
briefing.body: A shell flies in an arc. ENIAC finds the arc one small hop at a time, and punches a card after each hop. Each card is one dot. You will connect the dots.
briefing.more: ENIAC was built to work out firing tables for Army guns. It was shown to the public on February 15, 1946. Brian Stuart's program tries to recreate the demo from that day. Six women programmers set up ENIAC for it.

plan.headline: Hop by hop
plan.body: ENIAC finds a shell's path one hop at a time. Each hop: the air slows the shell, the shell moves, ENIAC punches a card, and checks the shell is still flying. Then it hops again.
plan.more: The air slows a fast shell a lot. ENIAC looks up how much in a table of numbers. Brian Stuart's note in the program says he tried to work that table out himself, so the table is his best attempt.
plan.math: card 1, card 2, card 3 ... one dot each

rest.headline: The rest is done for you
rest.body: Real ENIAC programmers placed hundreds of cables by hand, and setting up took days. We will place the last ones now: 293 cables and 1,147 switches. Most of the switches make up the drag table.

before.headline: Press READ
before.sub: READ pulls the card of numbers into ENIAC.

captions.text: The card goes through the reader.
The first number, 97,367, lands in Accumulator 1.
The other numbers wait inside ENIAC. Now press INIT.

before.headline: Press INIT
before.sub: INIT is the Initiating Pulse, ENIAC's GO button.

captions.text: Card 1 is out. Its big numbers say how far along and how high up the shell is.
Each hop, the air slows the shell, and gravity pulls it down.
Highest point! From here the shell comes down.
Landed! The height dropped below zero.

plot.stretch: Height stretched so you can see it.
plot.cross: where the line between the last two dots crosses the ground

run.note: ENIAC does a lot of arithmetic for every hop.

result.headline: ENIAC flew the shell!
result.body: Each card was one hop. Joined up, the dots show the whole flight: up, over the top, and down. ENIAC worked it out from a card of numbers and the cables you placed.
result.more: The real ENIAC could work out a trajectory like this much faster than a shell takes to fly. By hand, the same work took days. Our simulator is slower, so you can watch every hop.
result.takeaway: Numbers and cables made a flight path.
result.takeawaySub: That is what programming ENIAC meant.

live.waiting: The shell is still flying: hop {n}

credits: Brian L. Stuart, programs/trajdemo.e and programs/drag.e
